title: What Are Dreams For?
focus: Hedging and impersonal structures in academic English

lines.text: Right, let's make a start. Today's question is one that's been around for, well, roughly as long as there have been people asleep, which is to say forever: what are dreams actually for? And I should warn you at the outset that I'm not going to give you a tidy answer, because, frankly, there isn't one.

What I can do is walk you through the main contenders. And I'd ask you to bear in mind, as we go, that most of the evidence here is, shall we say, indirect. We can measure brain activity during sleep with considerable precision. What we can't do is see the dream itself. We rely on what people tell us when they wake up, and memory, as we discussed last week, is not the most reliable of witnesses.

So, contender number one. The idea that dreams have no function at all. On this view, sometimes called the activation-synthesis model, the sleeping brain fires off more or less random signals, and the higher parts of the brain do their best to stitch them into some kind of story. The dream, in other words, is a by-product. Rather like the noise a car engine makes. It tells you the engine's running, but the engine isn't running in order to make noise.
Sorry, can I just jump in? If dreams are random, why do so many people have the same kinds of dreams? Falling, being chased, turning up to an exam unprepared?

Good question, and it's precisely the one critics of that model tend to raise. The recurrence of certain themes across cultures would seem to suggest that something more than randomness is going on. Though, to be fair, defenders of the model would say that the brain's interpretive machinery is itself fairly uniform, so you'd expect similar stories to emerge from similar raw material. It's not a knockout blow either way.

Contender number two, and this is the one that's attracted most attention over the last couple of decades: dreams as a kind of overnight memory processing. There's reasonably good evidence that sleep, and in particular certain stages of sleep, plays a role in consolidating memories, in deciding, if you like, what to keep and what to throw away. And it's been suggested that dreaming may be the subjective experience of that sorting process.
So when I dream about my primary school with my current flatmates in it, that's my brain filing things?
Badly, in my case.
Well, the filing system's not known for its tidiness. But yes, that's one interpretation.
And is there any way of checking that?

Indirectly. People who are deprived of certain stages of sleep tend to do worse on memory tests the next day. That's suggestive. It doesn't tell us whether the dream itself matters, or just the sleep it happens in. Mixing old and new material is very characteristic of dreams, and it fits rather nicely with the idea that the brain is trying to integrate recent experience into older networks. I'd stress the word 'fits', though. Fitting the evidence isn't the same as being proven by it.

Then there's a third family of theories, which focus on emotion. The idea here is that dreams provide a sort of safe rehearsal space for threatening situations. You're chased, you escape, and you wake up having, in some sense, practised. Some researchers have gone further and argued that dreaming helps take the sting out of painful memories, that we revisit them in a context where the stress chemistry is turned down, so they become a bit less raw.
Is there any actual evidence for that, or is it just a nice story?

There's some. Not as much as one might like. There are studies suggesting that people who dream about a distressing experience tend to report feeling somewhat better about it the next day. But the samples are small, and it's notoriously hard to control for everything else going on in people's lives. So I'd put it in the 'promising but unconfirmed' category.
What about the idea that dreams have hidden meanings? The psychoanalytic stuff?

Ah. Yes. Well, it would be fair to say that the idea of dreams as disguised wishes, which you'll associate with Freud, has fallen rather out of favour in experimental circles, largely because it's so difficult to test. If a dream about a train can mean almost anything, then no dream can ever count as evidence against the theory. And a theory that nothing can contradict isn't, strictly speaking, a scientific one.

That said, I wouldn't want to dismiss the broader intuition entirely. Dreams do seem to draw on our concerns, our anxieties, the things we're preoccupied with. You don't need an elaborate symbolic code to see that someone worried about their job might dream about being late for work.
So which one do you think is right?

Honestly? I suspect it's a mistake to look for a single function. Evolution tends to be opportunistic. Something that arises for one reason gets co-opted for others. It's entirely possible that dreaming is partly a by-product, partly involved in memory and partly in emotional regulation, and that the proportions vary from person to person and night to night.

What I'd really like you to take away is a sense of how carefully claims in this area need to be worded. You'll notice I've said 'it would appear', 'there's some evidence', 'it's been suggested' rather a lot today. That's not me being evasive. It's an accurate reflection of where the science is.
It's a bit unsatisfying, though, isn't it?

It is. But I'd rather you left here unsatisfied and accurately informed than satisfied and misled. For next week, I'd like you to read the two papers on the reading list about dream recall and come prepared to tell me which of them you find more convincing, and, more importantly, why.

title: Is the Four-Day Week Here to Stay?
focus: Concession and contrast: albeit, notwithstanding, much as, however + adjective

lines.text: Good evening and welcome. Tonight's question: is the four-day week a genuine revolution in how we work, or a perk that only certain kinds of companies can afford? With me are Greg Holloway, a labour economist; Siobhan Kerr, who runs a design agency that switched to a four-day week two years ago; and Liam Torres, a union representative. Siobhan, you've actually done it. How's it gone?

Better than I expected, to be honest. Much as I'd like to claim I'd planned it all perfectly, we stumbled into it, really. We tried it as a three-month trial, fully expecting to go back. Output didn't drop. If anything, it went up slightly. People stopped wasting time in meetings because they knew they only had four days. And our sick days roughly halved.
Greg, is that typical?

It's consistent with what the larger trials have found, albeit with some important caveats. Most of the organisations that took part in those trials volunteered, which means they were probably the ones most likely to succeed. You don't get many companies saying, 'Yes, sign us up, we expect this to go terribly.' So I'd be cautious about generalising from them.
That's fair, but it cuts both ways. We volunteered because we were desperate. We were losing staff to bigger agencies. It wasn't idealism.

Sure, and I'm not dismissing your experience. However impressive the results, though, the question is whether they'd hold up in sectors where output is tied directly to hours. A hospital ward can't produce four days' worth of nursing in five days' worth of patients.

Can I come in there? Because that's exactly the point I'd make, but from the other side. Nobody serious is saying a nurse should just work twenty per cent less and somehow cover the same shifts. What we're saying is that the gains from productivity, which have been considerable over the last few decades, have gone almost entirely to employers. Working time hasn't really budged since the nineteen-seventies. A shorter week is one way of sharing those gains.
Notwithstanding the fairness argument, which I have some sympathy with, you still need someone to pay for the extra staff in the hospital.
Absolutely. And that's a political choice, not a law of nature.
Well, everything's a political choice if you go back far enough.
Fair enough. But some are rather more obviously political than others.
Siobhan, did anything go wrong?

Oh, plenty. Clients didn't love it at first. We had one who insisted on calling on Fridays, every single Friday, I think just to make a point. And some of the team found the four days quite intense. You do compress things. One of our junior designers told me she was more tired on Thursday evenings than she'd ever been on a Friday before.

Which is actually quite an important finding. Some studies suggest that a portion of the productivity gain comes from intensification, people simply working harder in fewer hours. That's fine up to a point. Beyond that point, you're just burning people out more efficiently.
Though, to be fair, that's a design problem, not an argument against the idea.
I'd go along with that, broadly.
A rare moment of consensus. Let's not waste it.
Liam, what about people who don't want it? Not everyone does.

True. We've got members who'd rather keep five shorter days, particularly parents who need to be there for the school run. So, no, it shouldn't be one-size-fits-all. The principle is reducing hours without reducing pay. The four-day week is just the most visible version of it.
That's what we found too, actually. We ended up with a couple of people doing four days and a couple doing five shorter days. It's messier to manage, I'll grant you. But it's held together.
Greg, final word from you. Is it here to stay?

In some sectors, I'd say yes, probably. Knowledge work, creative industries, places where hours were always a rather poor measure of output. Elsewhere, much as I'd like to be optimistic, I think it'll take a lot more than enthusiasm. It'll take investment, and it'll take political will. Whether we get either is, well, anyone's guess.
Thank you all. That's all we have time for tonight.

title: The River Beneath the Streets

lines.text: Standing on the corner of Mill Lane on a weekday morning, you'd have no idea there was a river here. There's traffic, a bus stop, a café selling overpriced sourdough. But if you crouch down by this drain cover and listen, you can just hear it. Water, moving fast, about four metres below the tarmac.

The Fleetbrook once ran openly through the centre of this town. Fed by springs in the hills to the north, it powered three mills, supplied the brewery and, by the eighteen-sixties, carried most of the town's sewage. Which is, more or less, why it disappeared.

My great-grandmother used to talk about the smell. She said in summer you couldn't open a window on this street. People were dying of cholera, and the river got the blame, quite rightly. So they bricked it over. Out of sight, out of mind.
Joan Pemberton has lived on Mill Lane all her life. Her house, built in eighteen eighty-two, stands almost directly over the old riverbed.
When it rains heavily, you can hear it rumbling under the floor. My husband used to say it was the ghosts of the millers. I'd say, no, love, it's the drains.

The culvert built to contain the Fleetbrook was, by the standards of its day, a triumph of engineering. Lined with brick, wide enough for a man to walk through, it carried the river for nearly two kilometres before releasing it into the estuary. For more than a century, nobody gave it much thought.
The trouble is, it was designed for Victorian rainfall. And Victorian rainfall isn't what we're getting.
Marcus Reid is a hydrologist working with the town council.

When you put a river in a pipe, you fix its capacity. It can carry so much water and no more. In twenty-nineteen, we had a storm that dumped almost a month's rain in six hours. The culvert simply couldn't cope. Water backed up, came out through the drains, and flooded about forty properties on this street and the two either side.
Including mine. Thirty centimetres of brown water in the front room. Having lived here seventy years, I'd never seen anything like it.
Since then, the council has been considering something that would have seemed unthinkable a generation ago. Opening the river up again.

We call it daylighting. It's been done in quite a few cities now, Seoul, Zurich, a couple in the States. You take a river that's been buried and you bring it back to the surface, give it a channel, some banks, room to spread when it needs to.
Dana Whitfield is an urban designer who's advised on several such projects.

The flood argument is the one that gets the funding. But honestly, it's not the only benefit. Cities that have done this find that the streets alongside become places people actually want to be. Property values go up. Wildlife comes back surprisingly quickly. And there's something about running water that just changes how people feel about a neighbourhood.
Not everyone is convinced. Opening the Fleetbrook would mean closing part of Mill Lane to traffic, and the businesses relying on passing trade are worried.
I can see both sides, I really can. The café owner, Kemal, he's been here twelve years. If the road shuts for two years of building work, he could go under.

That's a genuine concern, and we're not dismissing it. Any scheme approved would have to include support for affected businesses during construction. But we've also got to weigh that against the cost of doing nothing, which, given the forecasts, is likely to be another serious flood within the decade.
And there's the question of what, exactly, would come back to the surface.

People sometimes imagine a pristine mountain stream. It won't be that, at least not at first. Urban rivers carry runoff from roads, all sorts of pollution. The water quality has to be dealt with before you open anything up, otherwise you've just got a smelly ditch, and you've proved the Victorians right.
The council is due to decide next spring. For Joan, the decision is personal.
I'd like to see it before I go, if I'm honest. The actual river. My great-grandmother hated it, and she had good reason. But I think she'd be pleased to know it was clean enough to look at again.

Back at the drain cover on Mill Lane, the water is still running, invisible, unhurried, as it has for a hundred and fifty years. Whether it sees daylight again depends on decisions being made in the council chamber a few streets away. For now, you'll just have to listen.

title: The Nose Knows (Mostly)
focus: Modals of speculation and deduction (present, past, future)

lines.text: My guest today has one of the more unusual jobs I've come across. Rosa Delgado is a professional coffee taster, or cupper, to use the trade term. She can apparently tell you which hillside a bean was grown on. Rosa, is that true, or is that just good marketing?

Bit of both, honestly. On a good day, with a coffee I know well, I can often tell you the region, sometimes the farm. But I'd be lying if I said I never get it wrong. Anyone who claims they're never wrong must be either very lucky or not being entirely straight with you.
How did you end up doing this? It can't have been a career you planned at school.

No, definitely not. I was working in a café in Brisbane, pretty bored, and the owner started bringing in these little sample bags from different producers. He'd line them up and make us taste them blind. I was hopeless at first. Couldn't tell one from another. And then, after a few months, something clicked.
Clicked how?

It's hard to describe. It wasn't that I suddenly had a better tongue. I think what changed was attention. I started noticing things that must have been there all along. A sort of dried-apricot quality in some Ethiopian coffees, a kind of cocoa heaviness in others. Once you've got a name for something, you can't unnotice it.
So it's learned, not innate?

Mostly learned. There's some variation between people, obviously. Some folks are more sensitive to bitterness, for example. But the research I've read suggests that experts don't actually have more sensitive noses than anyone else. What they've got is a better vocabulary and a better memory for smells. They can retrieve the label faster.
I have to ask about the famous experiments with wine, where experts were given white wine dyed red and described it as if it were red.

Yeah, look, I love those experiments, and they're humbling. They show that expectation shapes perception enormously. If you see red, your brain goes looking for red-wine words. It'll happily find them. And I'm sure the same would happen to me with coffee if someone set me up cleverly enough.
Doesn't that undermine the whole profession?

I don't think so. It undermines the idea that tasting is pure, objective measurement. Which, fair enough, it isn't. But it doesn't mean we're making it up. That's why we taste blind whenever it matters. We take away the label, the price, the story on the packet. Then we've only got the cup.
Have you ever been badly caught out?

Oh, plenty of times. The worst was at a competition in Melbourne, years ago. I was absolutely convinced one sample was a Kenyan. Bright, acidic, blackcurrant, textbook Kenyan. Turned out it was from Colombia, from a farm that had been experimenting with a new variety. I must have gone the colour of a tomato. But it taught me something. My memory said Kenya, so I stopped tasting and started recognising. Those aren't the same thing.
What about the future? Could a machine do your job?

There are electronic noses being developed, and they'll probably get very good at detecting defects, things like mould or over-fermentation. That's useful. But whether a machine will ever tell you that a coffee tastes like your grandmother's kitchen on a winter morning, I'm not so sure. And that, in the end, is what people are paying for.
That's quite a romantic view for someone who's just told me how unreliable perception is.
Ha. Maybe. I'd say I'm a romantic with a spreadsheet. I believe in the experience, but I write everything down, because I don't trust my memory of it.
Last question. What should listeners do if they want to taste better?

Slow down. Taste two coffees side by side rather than one on its own; comparison does most of the work. And don't worry about the fancy words. If it reminds you of something, say so. You might well be right.
Rosa Delgado, thank you.
Pleasure. Now I need a coffee.

title: Glorious Flops
focus: Advanced verb patterns: gerund vs infinitive with change of meaning

lines.text: Welcome back to Glorious Flops, the podcast about products that should have changed the world and, er, didn't. I'm Kat.
And I'm Josh. And today, Kat, I believe you've brought me a personal favourite.
I have. Today we're talking about the self-heating soup can. Picture it: you're on a mountain, it's freezing, you pull a tab, and three minutes later you've got hot tomato soup. No stove, no fire.
That actually sounds brilliant.
It was brilliant. In theory. I remember seeing the advert as a kid and thinking it was the future. My dad bought a box for a camping trip.
And?

And I remember trying to open one in the tent and it sort of… fizzed. Then it got hot on one side and stayed stone cold on the other. My dad stopped to read the instructions, which nobody ever does, and it turned out you had to shake it for a full minute first.
Which, to be fair, is the kind of thing you'd put on the front of the can.

You would think so. It was in tiny print on the bottom. Anyway, the company had spent years trying to perfect the heating element, and the technology did work, mostly. What they forgot to do was ask whether people actually wanted to pay four times the price of normal soup for the privilege.
See, this is the thing that fascinates me about flops. It's rarely that the idea is stupid. It's that someone fell in love with solving a problem that customers didn't really feel they had.

Exactly. And there were safety issues, too. A few cans overheated. Nobody was seriously hurt, but there were reports of them bulging, and one apparently went off like a small firework in a supermarket in Ohio.
Oh no.
Oh yes. They tried recalling a batch, but by then the newspapers had got hold of it, and 'exploding soup' is the kind of headline that, once printed, you don't really recover from.
I'd like to go on to something you mentioned in your notes, because I think it's the interesting bit. The founder didn't just give up, did he?

No, and this is why I love this story. He regretted launching too early, he said so publicly, which founders almost never do. But he went on to sell the heating technology to a company making emergency meals for disaster relief.
Ah, so the soup can failed, but the idea found the right customer.
Right. People stuck after an earthquake, with no power and no gas, don't care that it costs four times as much. They care that it's hot.
That's a really nice reversal. It reminds me of what one of our guests said last season, that a flop is often just a good idea standing in the wrong room.
I remember that. I meant to steal that line for the intro and forgot.
Well, you've stolen it now. On air. I'll be sending you an invoice.
Put it on my tab. Before we wrap up, though, I want to give listeners the takeaway, because we always try to have one.
Go for it.

Stop asking 'Can we build it?' and start asking 'Who needs this badly enough to pay for it?' If the honest answer is 'campers who'll use it once', you might want to try finding a different customer before you try building a factory.
Wise words. Next week: the smart fork that told you off for eating too fast.
I genuinely cannot wait.

title: Twelve Strangers: Your Stories of Jury Service
focus: Unreal past: wish, if only, it's (high) time, would rather, as if

lines.text: You're listening to Midday Live, and this morning we're asking: have you served on a jury, and what was it really like? The lines have been busy since nine. Let's go straight to Gwen in Swansea. Gwen, good morning.
Morning, Martin. I did jury service about five years ago. A fraud case. Six weeks.
Six weeks! How did you feel when the letter arrived?
Honestly? I wished I'd never registered to vote. I had a small business, and I thought, how on earth am I going to manage? I'd much rather they'd picked someone retired.
And how did it turn out?

That's the strange thing. By the end, I was glad I'd done it. You sit there with eleven people you'd never otherwise meet, a bus driver, a vicar, a lad of nineteen, and you all have to agree on something that matters enormously to someone's life. I've never taken anything so seriously.
Did you reach a verdict?

We did, after two days. I won't say what. But I still think about the defendant sometimes. If only we'd been allowed to ask more questions ourselves. You feel as if you're watching a play where half the script's been cut.
That's a theme we've heard a lot this morning. Raj in Leicester, you've got a different take?

I have, yeah. I was on a jury for an assault case, and I came away feeling it's high time the system was reformed. Some of the jurors clearly hadn't followed the evidence. One woman said in the deliberation room that she'd decided on the first day because the defendant 'had shifty eyes'.
What did you do?
We argued with her, quite a lot. It took a whole afternoon. In the end, she came round. But I keep thinking: what if she hadn't? What if there'd been three of her?
So would you rather cases like that were decided by a judge alone?

Not exactly. I'd rather jurors were given a bit more guidance, about how to weigh evidence, about the difference between a hunch and a reason. It's as if they expect you to know all that already, just by being an adult.
Lorraine, you're calling from Bristol, but I'm guessing you're not from Bristol originally.
Ha, no, I moved here from Ohio fifteen years ago. I've done jury service in both countries, which I think is pretty rare.
That must give you an interesting perspective.

It does. The main difference is that in the States, the lawyers can question potential jurors before the trial and get rid of the ones they don't like. Here, you just turn up and you're on. I'd rather the British way, honestly. Back home it sometimes felt as though the case had been half-won before anyone said a word, just by picking the right twelve people.
And what about the experience itself? Was it similar?

Surprisingly, yes. That moment in the deliberation room when you realise nobody's coming to tell you the answer, that's universal. I remember wishing someone would just walk in and tell us what really happened. But nobody does. That's the whole point.
Gwen, you're still on the line. Do you recognise that?
Absolutely. It's the loneliest responsibility I've ever had, and I wasn't even alone.
We'll take a short break. After the news, a retired judge will be responding to some of your comments, including Raj's suggestion about guidance for jurors. Stay with us.

title: A Vault Against the End of the World
focus: Advanced passives: reporting passives and passive infinitives

lines.text: It's been called the world's agricultural insurance policy. Built into a mountainside on a remote Arctic archipelago, a seed vault holds more than a million samples of crops from almost every country on earth. Our science correspondent, Tom Ashby, has been given rare access. Tom.

Thanks. I'm standing at the entrance now, which is essentially a concrete wedge sticking out of the snow. It's minus fourteen out here, and the wind is, well, let's say bracing. Behind me is a tunnel running about a hundred and thirty metres into the rock. The seeds are kept at minus eighteen degrees, and the permafrost is supposed to keep them cold even if the power fails.
Supposed to?

Yes, and that's part of the story. A few years ago, warmer than expected temperatures caused meltwater to seep into the entrance tunnel. No seeds are reported to have been damaged, but it was a wake-up call. I'm joined by Ingrid Larsen, who works for the organisation that manages the vault.

Hello. Yes, the incident was taken very seriously. The tunnel has since been waterproofed and the drainage rebuilt. I'd stress that the vault itself was never in danger. But it was a reminder that even a facility designed to last for centuries has to be adapted to a climate that's changing faster than anyone planned for.
So, lesson learned?
Lesson very much learned. The tunnel is now monitored all year round, not just in the summer months.
What exactly is stored here?

Duplicates, mainly. Most countries have their own gene banks, and the vault is meant to be a backup for those. If a national collection is lost, through war, natural disaster or simple mismanagement, the seeds can be returned to the depositor. They remain the property of the country that sent them. We just look after them.
And has that ever actually happened?

It has. The first withdrawal was made by researchers whose gene bank had been forced to close because of conflict. Seeds that had been deposited a few years earlier were sent back, grown, and the new seeds produced were then redeposited. So the system was shown to work, which, frankly, was a relief.
I'm now inside the vault itself. It's eerily quiet, rows of shelves stacked with plain black boxes, each one sealed. Kofi Mensah is a plant geneticist who's visited from Ghana to deposit samples.

Hi. Yeah, I'm bringing varieties of sorghum and millet, crops that are thought to have been grown in our region for thousands of years. Some of them are only cultivated now by a handful of farmers. If those farmers stop, the varieties could be lost for good.
Why does that matter, if there are modern, higher-yielding varieties available?

Because the modern varieties are often quite uniform. They're bred for yield under ideal conditions. The older ones may be less productive, but some are believed to carry traits like drought tolerance or resistance to particular pests. As the climate changes, those traits could turn out to be enormously valuable. You don't know which genes you'll need in fifty years. So you keep as many as you can.
Is the vault the answer, then?

It's part of the answer. I'd be careful about thinking of it as a solution on its own. Seeds in a freezer don't evolve. In the field, crops keep adapting to new conditions, new diseases. Ideally you want both: seeds stored safely and seeds being grown, by farmers, every season.
I'd agree with that entirely. The vault is meant to be a last resort, not a first one.

Before I leave, I'm shown a box that's due to be deposited this afternoon. It contains a variety of bean that's said to have been saved by a single family, passed down through four generations. It'll now be kept here, in the dark and the cold, possibly for centuries. Ingrid, does this place ever feel strange to you?

All the time. You're preparing for disasters you hope will never happen. But I find it quite hopeful, actually. Someone in two hundred years might open one of these boxes and plant something that feeds a city. That's not a bad thing to have been part of.
From the Arctic, for now, back to you.
Tom Ashby, thank you. Fascinating stuff.

title: Is That Supposed to Be Funny?
focus: Ellipsis and substitution (so, not, do so, one)

lines.text: Right, so, the scene in the dentist's waiting room. Did you rewrite it?
I did. Well, I tried to. I'm not sure it's any better. Possibly worse.
Let's have a look. Hmm. You've cut the bit with the fish tank.
I have. Didn't you say it was too long?
I said the build-up was too long. Not the payoff. The fish tank was the best thing in it.
Was it? I thought you hated it.
I hated the first version. I loved the second one. You've cut the second one.
Ah. Right. Okay, I'll put it back. Do you want the shorter build-up with it or the longer?
The shorter, definitely. The audience gets it in two lines. We don't need four.
Fair. Although I'd argue the third line's doing something. It's where she starts suspecting the dentist isn't a real dentist.
Is it? I thought that came later.
No, it's set up there. If you cut it, the reveal at the end doesn't land.
Hmm. I suppose so. Fine, keep the third line, lose the fourth.
Deal. What about the receptionist? Is she working for you?
She's working, but she's not funny yet. She's just efficient. Comedy characters need a want. What does she want?
To go home?
Everyone wants to go home. That's not a want, that's a Tuesday.
Okay, okay. What if she's desperately trying to get the dentist to notice her, and he never does so, because he's obsessed with the fish?
Oh, I like that. That ties the fish tank in properly. It's not just a gag any more.
Exactly. And the fish could be the one thing he's genuinely good at caring for. Which is sort of sad, actually.
Sad is good. The best comedy's always got a sad one hiding underneath it somewhere.
Do you think the producers will go for sad?
I think not, if we pitch it as sad. If we pitch it as funny and it happens to be sad, they'll never notice.
Ha. That's very cynical.
It's very practical. Same thing, in this business.
Okay, I'll do another pass tonight. Fish back in, third line stays, receptionist in love with an oblivious dentist.
Perfect. And Dev? Don't cut anything else without asking me.
I won't. Probably.
